title: Stage 1: Chirp from 1 to 100 users
scopeHtml: Scope: one VM with app and Postgres, monolith, layered code, backups, entities and layers. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: Load and goal
notes.html:
Chirp is a Twitter-style service: users post short text or image posts, follow others, read a home timeline, search, and get notifications. This master track scales ONE app from 0 to 1 billion users. Every stage has a number that forces the next change; we never add a box "because big companies have it".

Stage 1: 1 to 100 users. Goal: ship and learn. Not "scale". The only requirements are: it works, it does not lose data, and you can rebuild it if the machine dies.

Worked example (the load). 100 users, maybe 30 active a day, each opening the app 10 times and posting once: about 300 page loads and 30 posts per day. That is 330 requests divided by 86,400 s, roughly 0.004 requests/s on average. Even a very bad peak (everyone at once, 10 requests/s) is trivial for one small VM. The goal of this stage is therefore simplicity, not capacity.

Industry examples. Instagram launched as a Django app plus Postgres on very few machines. Basecamp and Stack Overflow ran monoliths on a handful of servers for years. Twitter itself began as a single Rails monolith.

Everyday analogy. A food stall: one person cooks, serves and takes money. No manager, no shifts. Perfect until the queue reaches the next street.

Common interview traps.

  • Starting the answer at "microservices, Kafka, sharding". At 100 users that is waste and risk.
  • Not stating the starting numbers. Always say "0.004 requests per second" out loud; it shows the interviewer you reason from load.

notes.title: Configuration
notes.html:
Concrete setup for Stage 1. Everything lives on one VM.

Item Value
Cloud AWS (any cloud is fine)
VM t3.small (2 vCPU burstable, 2 GB RAM), Ubuntu 22.04 LTS
Disk 30 GB gp3 EBS, encrypted; 3,000 IOPS baseline
Reverse proxy Nginx 1.24 terminating TLS (Let's Encrypt, certbot auto-renew)
App Kotlin + Spring Boot 3, one JVM, -Xms512m -Xmx768m
Database PostgreSQL 16 on the same VM, shared_buffers=256MB, work_mem=4MB, max_connections=50
App DB pool HikariCP maximumPoolSize=10
Images Local directory /var/chirp/media served by Nginx
Deploy git pull plus systemctl restart chirp; later a tiny GitHub Actions script
Backups Nightly pg_dump to S3 at 03:00, retention 14 days; daily EBS snapshot, retention 7

Nginx config (the only proxy rules you need):

server {
  listen 443 ssl http2;
  server_name chirp.example.com;
  client_max_body_size 5m;               # image upload limit

  location /media/ { alias /var/chirp/media/; expires 7d; }
  location /api/   { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8080; proxy_read_timeout 15s; }
}

Backup script (cron 0 3 * * *):

#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
F=/tmp/chirp-$(date +%F).dump
pg_dump -Fc -U chirp chirp > "$F"
aws s3 cp "$F" s3://chirp-backups/daily/ --storage-class STANDARD_IA
rm "$F"

Common interview traps.

  • Leaving max_connections at 100 with a pool of 100 "to be safe". Postgres processes are heavy (about 5 to 10 MB each); a small pool is faster.
  • Taking backups but never restoring one. A backup you have not restored is a hope, not a backup.

notes.title: Decision and why
notes.html:
Four decisions, each with options considered.

Decision 1: monolith vs microservices. Options: (a) one deployable app, (b) split into user, post, timeline, notification services. Chosen: (a). With 2 developers, a network call between services costs more (latency, deploys, versioning, debugging) than it saves. A monolith is one deploy, one transaction, one log file.

Decision 2: Postgres vs MySQL vs MongoDB. Chirp's data is relational (users, follows, posts). Options: Postgres (strong SQL, JSONB, great indexes), MySQL (also fine, slightly simpler replication at the time), MongoDB (flexible documents, but joins and transactions across follows are harder). Chosen: Postgres, because we want transactions and ad-hoc queries today and good full-text search (tsvector) for the first search feature.

Decision 3: one VM vs managed services. Options: (a) one VM with everything, (b) RDS plus separate app. Chosen: (a) now because cost is about $25 a month and nothing is blocked. The price is that the database shares CPU and RAM with the app, which is fixed in Stage 2.

Decision 4: store images on local disk vs S3. Local disk is simplest and Nginx serves it fast. It becomes a trap the moment there are two app servers (Stage 3), so we keep image access behind one interface MediaStore so the move is a code swap, not a rewrite.

Industry examples. Instagram's early Postgres choice stayed for over a decade. Shopify's core is still a modular monolith, now with strict module boundaries. Segment famously moved from microservices back to a monolith because of operations cost.

Everyday analogy. Buying a bicycle before a car: you learn the roads first.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "monolith" as if it were bad. The interview answer is "monolith first, with clean layers, split only when a real bottleneck or team boundary forces it".
  • Choosing a NoSQL store "for scale" when the data is relational and tiny.

notes.title: Alternatives (branches)
notes.html:
Options we considered and rejected for Stage 1, and what would make us pick them.

Alternative Why not now When it wins
Serverless (Lambda plus DynamoDB) Cold starts, no relational queries, vendor lock-in for a team that does not need it Spiky, tiny traffic with near-zero ops staff
PaaS (Heroku, Render, Fly) Fine choice; slightly more per month, less control If nobody on the team wants to manage a VM
Docker Compose on the VM Adds a layer but gives reproducible deploys Fine, optional; we keep systemd for fewer moving parts
Kubernetes Huge ops cost for one process 30+ services, many teams
Managed Postgres (RDS) from day one About $15 to $60 more a month, saves backup/patch work Chosen in Stage 2

Everyday analogy. Renting a furnished flat (PaaS) versus an empty one (VM): same walls, different effort.

Common interview traps.

  • Presenting only your chosen option. Interviewers score you on the options you rejected and why.
  • Treating Kubernetes as the default. It solves orchestration for many services, not "a first app".

notes.title: What breaks next
notes.html:
The signals that tell you Stage 1 is over (and which metric shows each):

  1. DB and app fight for RAM. Symptom: random slow requests, swap usage rising, JVM GC pauses plus Postgres cache misses. Metric: free -m swap used above 0, pg_stat_database.blks_read rising.
  2. A slow query takes the CPU. A timeline query without an index scans the whole posts table. At 100 users it is invisible; at 1,000 users with 50,000 posts it takes 200 ms and burns a core.
  3. One VM is a single point of failure. If the VM or disk dies you lose up to a day of data (last nightly backup). Metric: your RPO (recovery point objective) is 24 hours.
  4. Deploys cause downtime. systemctl restart drops requests for about 15 s.

Common interview traps.

  • Predicting "we will need sharding next". The real next problems are boring: RAM contention, missing indexes, backups.
  • Ignoring RPO/RTO. Say them as numbers: RPO 24 h and RTO about 1 h now.

notes.title: Cost
notes.html:
Item Monthly
t3.small on-demand about $15
30 GB gp3 $2.4
S3 backups (a few GB) $0.5
Domain plus DNS about $2
EBS snapshots about $1
Data transfer about $2
Total about $25 per month

Cost per user at 100 users: $0.25 per month. This is fine because nothing here scales with users yet; the number only matters later.

Industry example. Early startups commonly run their first year on $20 to $50 a month. The scarce resource is developer time, not servers.

Common interview traps.

  • Quoting cost without a unit. Say "dollars per month" and "dollars per 1,000 users".

notes.title: LLD view
notes.html:
The first low-level design of Chirp: entities and layers. This is the code structure that must survive all ten stages.

Entities.

User(id, handle, display_name, email, password_hash, created_at)
Post(id, author_id -> User, body (<=280 chars), media_key?, created_at)
Follow(follower_id -> User, followee_id -> User, created_at)   PK(follower_id, followee_id)
Notification(id, user_id -> User, type, ref_post_id?, actor_id?, read_at?, created_at)

Layers.

HTTP controller   (parse, validate, map to DTO)       <- knows HTTP only
   |
Service           (rules: follow limits, 280 chars)   <- the "business" layer
   |
Repository        (SQL via JDBC / JPA)                <- knows Postgres only
   |
Postgres

MediaStore (interface) -> LocalDiskMediaStore  (later S3MediaStore)

Key interfaces (Kotlin):

interface PostRepository {
    fun save(post: Post): Post
    fun timelineFor(userId: Long, limit: Int, before: Long?): List<Post>
}

interface MediaStore {
    fun put(key: String, bytes: ByteArray)
    fun urlFor(key: String): String
}

class PostService(private val posts: PostRepository, private val media: MediaStore) {
    fun create(authorId: Long, body: String, image: ByteArray?): Post {
        require(body.length in 1..280) { "post must be 1..280 chars" }
        val key = image?.let { "img/${System.nanoTime()}.jpg".also { k -> media.put(k, it) } }
        return posts.save(Post(authorId = authorId, body = body, mediaKey = key))
    }
}

Table for the timeline and its first index:

CREATE TABLE posts (
  id         BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  author_id  BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
  body       VARCHAR(280) NOT NULL,
  media_key  TEXT,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX posts_author_created ON posts (author_id, created_at DESC);

The timeline at this stage is a simple pull query joining follows and posts:

SELECT p.* FROM posts p
JOIN follows f ON f.followee_id = p.author_id
WHERE f.follower_id = :me
ORDER BY p.created_at DESC LIMIT 50;

Why this matters later. Because services depend on the PostRepository and MediaStore interfaces, Stage 4 can put a cache behind the repository and Stage 5 can swap the media store, without touching controllers.

Industry examples. Layered (and hexagonal/ports-and-adapters) structure is the standard in Spring, Rails and Django shops; Shopify's modular monolith enforces module boundaries with tooling.

Everyday analogy. A restaurant: the waiter (controller) never cooks, the chef (service) never goes to the farm, the supplier (repository) never talks to customers.

Common interview traps.

  • Putting SQL in controllers. It makes the later cache or replica routing a rewrite.
  • Storing the media path as a full URL instead of a key, which makes the later CDN move painful.

notes.title: Decision gravity
notes.html:
Decision Gravity Why
Monolith Reversible (two-way door) Modules can be extracted later; cost is moderate if layers are clean
Postgres as primary store Mostly one-way Moving a live database engine is a multi-month project; choose carefully
Relational schema (ids, follows table) One-way-ish IDs and keys leak into every stage; BIGINT ids chosen now to avoid a later migration from INT
One VM Reversible Replaced in Stage 2 in about an hour
Local disk for images Reversible if behind MediaStore, painful otherwise Key-not-URL rule keeps it cheap
Nightly pg_dump Reversible Replaced by continuous WAL archiving in Stage 2

Rule of thumb used throughout this track: cheap-to-undo decisions are made fast; one-way doors get a written reason.

Common interview traps.

  • Using INT (max 2.1 billion) for post IDs. At 1B users it overflows; use BIGINT from day one.

notes.title: Concepts learned
notes.html:
• Monolith vs microservices; "monolith first".
  • Layered architecture: controller, service, repository, and ports (interfaces) for storage.
  • Back-of-envelope load: users to requests per second.
  • RPO and RTO; the difference between a backup and a tested restore.
  • Why identifiers are BIGINT, and why media is stored by key, not URL.
  • Connection pools exist and Postgres connections are expensive.

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing a backup with replication. Replication copies mistakes (a DELETE replicates instantly); backups let you go back in time.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Stage 1 (1 to 100 users): one t3.small VM running Nginx, one Spring Boot monolith and Postgres 16; about $25 per month.
  • Choose simplicity: the load is about 0.004 requests/s; the scarce resource is developer time.
  • Four entities (User, Post, Follow, Notification) and four layers (controller, service, repository, store) are the code skeleton for all later stages.
  • Use BIGINT ids, store media keys not URLs, and hide storage behind interfaces so later changes are cheap.
  • Nightly pg_dump to S3 gives RPO 24 h; test the restore.
  • Next bottleneck: DB and app fighting for RAM and CPU, plus single point of failure, so Stage 2 splits the database out.
